text: We are fighting for Cyrillic to be associated with Bulgaria, Albena Spasova told BTA (04.05.2026 17:27)

We are fighting to ensure that the Cyrillic script is associated precisely with Bulgaria, beyond the popular idea that we are talking about a Russian alphabet because of Russia’s large population, as well as to continue creating our own typefaces. It was truly important that Cyrillic became one of Europe’s three official scripts precisely through Bulgaria, with Bulgaria’s accession to the European Union. This was stated to BTA by Albena Spasova, a lecturer at the National Academy of Art (NAA), who gave a lecture in Mexico on April 22 related to the project “The Letters of Bulgaria – The Alphabet of Europe.” According to her, the presentation was structured as “a walk through the history of the world poster,” featuring 30 authors who hold a leading place in this field.

“I had constructed the lecture so that it contained an introductory part about the entire project, followed by two slides for each author, in which, in addition to the project poster, there were also between three and five of their iconic posters,” Spasova explained. She added that within 60 minutes, a “concise but very interesting presentation” was delivered, which has already been published on the website of the International Triennial of the Stage Poster. According to her, the sustained interest in the project is due both to the universal language of the poster and to the topic of Cyrillic. “The letter has always been a challenge for the poster designer… this is yet another opportunity to enrich the language of the poster,” the curator noted. She emphasized that the collection brings together “the cream of the world poster scene,” with the participants’ works being part of major international museums.

Participation in Mexico is part of a large-scale international festival in which Bulgaria has been a highlight. In addition to the exhibition, displays dedicated to Bulgarian cultural heritage, rose oil, and tourism were also presented. As part of the event, the Bulgarian artist Gredi Assa was awarded the title of “international honorary professor.”

Albena Spasova noted that the event opens up opportunities for future cooperation, including the participation of Bulgarian students in international initiatives in the fields of poster design and photography. She also emphasized the role of the Bulgarian embassy in the realization of the project, describing the presentation as “glamorous and very impressive.”

The international poster campaign **“The Letters of Bulgaria – Alphabet of Europe,”** created by the International Triennial of the Stage Poster in 2007, brings together 30 artists from 20 countries around the idea of visually representing the Bulgarian alphabet as one of the three writing systems in Europe. The collection includes 30 posters — one for each letter, assigned by lot during the fifth edition of the triennial in Sofia. The project combines the creative efforts of established poster artists from around the world and Bulgarian authors, with one of the letters — **“Ь”** — created through a competition among young Bulgarian artists. All works were produced in a unified format and typography and printed in several languages in a limited edition. The initiative aims to promote Bulgarian culture through contemporary art, turning the letters into a universal visual code. The collection has been presented in a number of international cultural centers.
